Q8060.L1t: Jurisprudence is the study of the nature, sources and function of law, and different schools define it in different ways.
Q8060.L2t: Analytical positivism treats law as it is actually laid down by human authority, separate from what morality says it ought to be.
Q8060.L3t: The phrase comes from the author of 'The Province of Jurisprudence Determined', who defined law as the command of a sovereign backed by sanction and confined jurisprudence to the study of such positive law.
Q8060.L4t: The definition of jurisprudence as the philosophy of positive law is credited to the founder of the English analytical school, who defined law as the sovereign's command.
Q8060.L2f: The phrase 'philosophy of positive law' first appeared in medieval canon law treatises, where it was used to contrast earthly statutes with divine law.
Q8060.L3f: The author of 'The Nature and Sources of the Law' is the thinker who defined jurisprudence as the philosophy of positive law.
Q8060.L4f: The definition of jurisprudence as the philosophy of positive law belongs to the American jurist who wrote 'The Nature and Sources of the Law'.

Q5868.L1t: Inequalities and intervals describe sets of real numbers on the number line, and conditions can be combined by taking intersections.
Q5868.L2t: The interval (-∞,-1) contains every real number strictly less than -1, so a number is outside it exactly when it is at least -1.
Q5868.L3t: Requiring 2u not to be below -1 means 2u ≥ -1, so u ≥ -1/2, and the matching condition on -20u gives a bound on the other side that must be intersected with this one.
Q5868.L4t: The set of such u is the closed interval running from negative one half to negative one twentieth.
Q5868.L2f: The set (-∞,-1) is a bounded interval that contains both of its endpoints.
Q5868.L3f: Neither 2u nor -20u falls in (-∞,-1) exactly when the absolute value of u is at most 1, since multiplying by 2 or -20 does not change which side of -1 the product lies on.
Q5868.L4f: The set of such u is the closed interval from negative one to positive one.

Q8222.L1t: Transplant recipients take immunosuppressive drugs to prevent rejection, and this makes them susceptible to opportunistic infections.
Q8222.L2t: Cyclosporine, azathioprine and prednisone suppress T-cell immunity, and anti-CD3 therapy depletes T cells further, which allows latent viruses to reactivate.
Q8222.L3t: A polyomavirus that stays latent in renal tissue reactivates under heavy immunosuppression and causes tubulointerstitial nephritis in the transplanted kidney, with a rising creatinine that mimics rejection.
Q8222.L4t: Her illness is best explained by reactivation of the polyomavirus BK virus in the transplanted kidney.
Q8222.L2f: Anti-CD3 monoclonal therapy works by depleting B cells, so its main effect is to remove antibody production while leaving T-cell function untouched.
Q8222.L3f: The usual cause of graft nephritis with rising creatinine after kidney transplantation is the alphaherpesvirus that stays latent in sensory ganglia and causes oral and genital blisters.
Q8222.L4f: Herpes simplex virus best explains her presentation.
